title: Grundy-value computation versus strategic determination
formal:
Historical general-reduction question, answered negatively by the source under the explicit assumption \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{PSPACE}\): for every succinctly represented terminating impartial normal-play ruleset, can its Grundy value be computed by a deterministic polynomial-time procedure using strategic determination for that same ruleset as an oracle?

The source exhibits Undirected Geography as an obstruction. Its strategic determination is polynomial-time computable, whereas computing its Grundy value is PSPACE-hard, even on planar bipartite graphs of maximum degree four. Consequently, a general reduction of the stated kind would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{PSPACE}\). This entry records that published conditional answer; it does not claim a proof that those complexity classes are different.

source_formulation.text: Is there a general polynomial-time reduction from Grundy-value computation to strategic determination?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

context:
The paper introduces Open Questions 1–6 to explain what its results settle. The saved Open Question 4 is followed by the paper’s negative result under the standard separation assumption, so its placement in an open-question paragraph did not justify retaining an unresolved catalogue entry.

Knowing whether a Grundy value is zero determines whether the player to move can win. Determining which positive value occurs can be substantially harder. The source’s Undirected Geography theorem demonstrates this distinction even though finding winning moves is efficient.

For the disjunctive sum of impartial games, a move changes exactly one component and the Grundy value of the sum is the bitwise XOR of component values. This explains why full Grundy information can be useful beyond winning an isolated component. The general-reduction question here concerns access to strategic determination for the original ruleset, not an oracle for arbitrary sums.

The paper proves the hardness and the resulting implication to \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{PSPACE}\). It does not prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{PSPACE}\), nor does it rule out reductions for individual rulesets whose strategic determination is already sufficiently hard.
why: The result shows that an efficiently playable impartial game need not have an efficiently computable algebraic summary for interaction with other games. It separates the information needed to win a component from the information captured by its complete Sprague–Grundy value.
status_note: The source itself supplies the conditional negative answer after posing its historical Open Question 4. Checked the full FOCS paper’s definitions, contribution statements and Theorem III.1, and the author preprint record; searched for later accounts. “Resolved” records the paper’s conditional impossibility result under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{PSPACE}\), not an unconditional separation of these classes. No independent proof verification.

sentences: An impartial game has a Grundy value that records more than whether the next player can win.
The historical question asks whether that value can always be computed efficiently using a procedure that finds winning moves.
Undirected Geography has polynomial-time strategic determination but PSPACE-hard Grundy computation.
The cited paper therefore rules out the proposed general reduction unless P equals PSPACE.
This is a conditional answer already present in the original source.

references.title: Winning the War by (Strategically) Losing Battles: Settling the Complexity of Grundy-Values in Undirected Geography
references.authors: Kyle W. Burke (Plymouth State University, USA), Matthew T. Ferland (University of Southern California, USA), Shang-Hua Teng (University of Southern California, USA)

definitions:
An impartial normal-play ruleset specifies positions and legal successor positions, with the same available moves for either player. The players alternate moves; a player with no legal move loses. Termination means that no play is infinite. A succinct representation encodes positions by finite binary strings, with a fixed algorithm enumerating their legal successors in time polynomial in the position’s encoding length. As in the source, all positions reachable from a position of length \(n\) have encoding length bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(n\). The ruleset and these algorithms are fixed, rather than part of each game input. The source’s obstruction already has a polynomial bound on play length.

The Grundy value is the nonnegative integer defined recursively by
\[
g(x)=\operatorname{mex}\{g(y):y\text{ is a legal successor of }x\},
\]
where \(\operatorname{mex}(S)=\min(\mathbb N_{0}\setminus S)\) and \(\operatorname{mex}(\varnothing)=0\). Termination and finite branching make the recursion well-founded. The value is at most the number of immediate legal successors, so its binary output is short in the stated representation. A position is losing exactly when its Grundy value is zero.

Strategic determination returns LOSING for a losing position; for a winning position it returns WINNING and one legal successor from which the next player loses. Thus it includes finding a winning move, not just deciding the winner.

The reduction under discussion is a deterministic polynomial-time Turing reduction, allowed polynomially many adaptive oracle calls on polynomial-length valid positions of the same fixed ruleset. Its ordinary computation, query writing and output are charged. The oracle must give correct strategic answers; any returned winning move is valid. A general reduction would have to work for every such ruleset. Even permitting a different polynomial-time reduction for each fixed ruleset cannot avoid the source’s obstruction unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{PSPACE}\). An oracle for a different, harder ruleset is outside this comparison.

In Undirected Geography, a position is an explicitly encoded finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a distinguished vertex \(s\) carrying a token. A move selects a neighbor \(t\) of \(s\), removes \(s\) and all its incident edges, and leaves the token at \(t\). A position with no neighbor at the token is terminal. Each move removes one vertex, so play lasts fewer than \(|V|\) moves. All graph positions are allowed. Restricting the hard instances to planar bipartite graphs with maximum degree four means that they can be drawn without crossings, their vertices split into two independent sets, and each vertex has at most four neighbors.

The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time; \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) uses polynomial working space. PSPACE-hardness of Grundy computation here means that exact computation would permit polynomial-time solutions of all PSPACE decision problems. The source in fact proves hardness of distinguishing particular small positive Grundy values. Hence this is a computational separation rather than an obstacle caused by writing a large integer.
answer_criterion: The recorded answer is the conditional refutation: assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{PSPACE}\), the proposed general polynomial-time reduction does not exist. A ruleset with polynomial-time strategic determination but PSPACE-hard Grundy computation supplies the required obstruction, and the source proves that Undirected Geography has these properties. The assumption must remain part of the conclusion.
